Question: Both roots of the quadratic equation \[x^2 - 63x + k = 0\] are prime numbers. The number of possible values of \(k\) is
Solution:
Let the prime roots be \(p\) and \(q\). A monic quadratic with these roots factors as \((x-p)(x-q)\). Expanding explains how its coefficients determine the sum and product:
\[
(x-p)(x-q)=x^2-(p+q)x+pq.
\]
Comparing with \(x^2-63x+k\), we obtain
\[
p+q=63,\qquad pq=k.
\]
Two odd numbers have an even sum, so the odd sum \(63\) requires one of the primes to be even. The only even prime is \(2\), making the other prime \(63-2=61\).

To check that \(61\) is prime, any composite \(61\) would have a prime divisor at most \(\sqrt{61}<8\). None of \(2,3,5,7\) divides it. Thus \(2\) and \(61\) are indeed both prime, and
\[
k=2\cdot61=122.
\]
The factorization \((x-2)(x-61)=x^2-63x+122\) confirms this value works. Every possible prime pair was forced to be this same pair, and exchanging the roots gives no new product. Hence there is exactly \(\boxed{1}\) possible value of \(k\), choice B.
